newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. holds "difficult" talks with Afghan factions.
newsitem.headline: U.N. holds "difficult" talks with Afghan factions.

text.p: Warring Afghan factions ended two days of talks in Islamabad on Wednesday but made little progress towards a ceasefire, U.N. envoy Norbert Holl said.

He told a news conference a working group of delegates from the purist Islamic Taleban militia and opposition factions had been unable to make headway on his ceasefire proposal because of disagreements over the timing of a prisoner exchange.
"The negotiations were very difficult," Holl said, noting that they coincided with fresh fighting between the Taleban and an opposition Shi'ite Moslem faction in central Afghanistan.
The Taleban launched a big offensive north of Kabul the day after the working group first met in Islamabad in mid-January, driving their foes to the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains.
"Both sides agreed that a military solution of the Afghanistan conflict was not possible," said a U.N. communique which Holl said had been discussed by the participants.

Holl said that even a decisive victory by one side would not end the Afghan conflict, which he predicted would spring up again in a different form, as in neighbouring Tajikistan, where Islamist rebels are fighting a Moscow-backed government.

Political analysts said the Taleban, who currently hold the military initiative in Afghanistan, had little interest in halting their drive to control the whole country and impose their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law.
Holl said he had tried to impress on the working group that only a political solution could lead to peace.

"Once the time of war is over, the time of reconstruction begins," he said. "You may be capable of demolishing the country alone, but you will not be able to build it up alone. For that you need international solidarity and cooperation."
The Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, said on Tuesday their fighters were mopping up resistance in territory newly gained from the Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat militia.
The militia's information minister, Amir Khan Mutaqi, told reporters at the frontline in Parwan province, northwest of Kabul, that the Sheikh Ali valley was under Taleban control.
Contradicting a report on Taleban-controlled radio, he said the militia had not yet captured the Shibar Pass, seen as a gateway to opposition-held northern and central Afghanistan.
A Hezb-i-Wahdat representative, Rasul Talib, took part in the Islamabad talks alongside General Mohammed Painda from northern General Abdul Rashid Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli group.
Bad weather prevented the representative of former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood from joining them.
The three-man Taleban delegation was led by Mullah Mohammed Sadiq, a member of the group's supreme shura (council).
Holl said he planned to meet the leaders of the rival groups soon to explain undisclosed new proposals, adding that he hoped progress could be made soon on confidence-building measures.
